1000598.etyen:
Internationalism, based on French Algérie (“Algeria”), from Alger (“Algiers”) and the country-name suffix -ie (“country-name suffix”). The city name is ultimately derived from Arabic اَلْجَزَائِر (al-jazāʔir, “the islands”), referring to four islands formerly lying off the city and later joined to the mainland.
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nynorsk Algerie, Danish Algeriet, Swedish Algeriet, German Algerien, Dutch Algerije and English Algeria.

1000854.etyen: From ut (“out, offshore”) + the older island name Sira. The first element refers to the island's position far out at sea. The origin of Sira is uncertain; it has been connected with the same root as se (“to see”), because the island is visible far out at sea, with Old Norse sær (“sea”) and Norwegian sjø (“sea”), perhaps originally referring to the open sea between Utsira and Karmøy, or with sige (“to flow slowly”), referring to current conditions.

en.g: a surname from English, a patronymic originally meaning “son of Jacob”

1001366.etyen:
Borrowed from English Jacobson (“patronymic surname meaning “son of Jacob””), from Jacob (“male given name”) + -son (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””). It may also represent an anglicized form of Scandinavian Jacobsen or Swedish Jacobsson.
Compare Swedish Jacobsson and Danish Jacobsen (“patronymic surnames”).

1004438.etyen:
From fy (“fie, ugh”) + faen (“the Devil; damn, fuck”).
The first element fy continues Old Norse fy, originally an imitative interjection representing a spitting sound, reflecting the old practice of spitting when naming evil powers. The second element faen is a contraction of fanden (“the Devil”), from late Old Norse fendinn (“the Devil”). The further origin of fendinn is uncertain; it is probably connected with Frisian or Middle Low German forms meaning “the tempter”, while influence from fjándi (“enemy; devil”) has also been proposed. en.g: a female given name from Latin [in turn from Old High German, in turn from Proto-Germanic], equivalent to English Ottilie

1004694.etyen:
Variant spelling of Otilie, from the German name tradition. The name goes back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, Latinised forms of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending. The spelling with th is historical and does not represent a separate /θ/ sound in Norwegian.
Compare Danish Othilie, Swedish Othilie, German Ottilie and English Ottilie (“female given name”).

1004950.etyen: polar (“polar”) + hare (“hare”), literally “polar hare”. The first element, polar, is ultimately from New Latin polaris (“polar”), from Latin polus (“pole”), from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis, pole”), from Proto-Hellenic *pólos (“axis, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷól-os (“turning, axis”), ultimately from *kʷel- (“to turn”). The second element, hare (“hare”), is inherited from Inherited from Old Norse heri (“hare”), from Proto-Germanic *hesô (“hare”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂s-én- (“hare”); the Germanic word may also have been associated with *haswaz (“grey”), compare Old Norse
